title: The sulphur baths of Abanotubani
tagline: Hot sulphur water under brick domes where the city was founded — a public room for a few lari, a private one for a group, and a scrub that takes a layer off.
when: a weekday afternoon; book a private room a few days ahead, more at weekends
why: The legend says a king's hunting falcon fell into a hot spring here and the city followed; whatever the truth, the springs are why Tbilisi is where it is — 'tbili' means warm. Abanotubani, the bath quarter under Narikala's rock at the mouth of the Legvtakhevi gorge, is a huddle of brick domes with the baths sunk beneath them, fed by water that comes out of the ground close to forty degrees and smelling of eggs. There are a handful of working houses: the blue-tiled Chreli Abano (the 'colourful' or Orbeliani bath) that everyone photographs, Gulo's, No. 5, the Royal, and plainer public rooms where locals pay by the hour. Pushkin and Dumas both wrote about them. The ritual is the same everywhere: soak, sweat, then a 'kisa' scrub by an attendant with a rough mitt and a bucket of soap foam, then soak again and drink tea. It is the one thing in Tbilisi that has not changed with the tourists, only got pricier.
take: Go twice. First, a public room — segregated by sex, cheap, no booking, full of Georgians talking, and the truest version of the thing. Second, a private room with three or four friends: a pool, a shower and a small dressing room for an hour, with the scrub added per person. That version is our favourite winter Smileys outing, and the conversation afterwards is different from any bar. Bring flip-flops and a towel or rent them; leave jewellery at home, because sulphur blackens silver. Skip it in August unless you enjoy sweating before you start. Chreli Abano takes online bookings (booking.chreli-abano.ge) and speaks English; the smaller houses want a phone call in Georgian or Russian, so ask a local member. Check the hours of the house you pick: most run from early morning to around midnight, but the public rooms keep their own schedules.

sections.title: How to do it
items: Public room: pay at the door, bring your own towel and flip-flops (or rent), and expect strangers to talk to you.
Private room: book ahead, three to five people, an hour; order the kisa scrub per person — it is the point.
Legvtakhevi: walk up the gorge behind the domes to the small waterfall before or after.
Metro: Avlabari is ten minutes' walk across the Metekhi bridge; Liberty Square is fifteen through the Old Town.
Sulphur and silver don't mix — leave the rings at home.

title: Old Town, the cable car and the rock where Narikala should be
tagline: Balconied lanes, a ropeway over the river to the Mother of Georgia, the botanical garden behind — and an honest note that the fortress itself is closed for restoration.
when: late afternoon, so the ride down is at dusk; avoid Sunday midday
why: Kala, the Old Town, is the wedge between Freedom Square and the river: crooked lanes, houses with carved wooden balconies leaning over the street, an Armenian church, Georgian churches, a mosque where Sunni and Shia pray together, a synagogue, and a pace that quickens every year as guesthouses, wine shops and 'Georgian feast' restaurants multiply. Above it on the ridge sits Narikala, the fortress the Persians started in the fourth century, and the aluminium Mother of Georgia (Kartlis Deda), sword in one hand and wine bowl in the other, from 1958. The cable car from Rike Park on the Avlabari side swings you over the Mtkvari and the roofs to the ridge in two minutes. The thing to say plainly: the fortress has been shut for a state-funded rehabilitation since 2024, completion dates in 2025 came and went, and as of this writing it is still closed with no announced reopening. The ridge, the statue, the viewpoints and the National Botanical Garden below the walls are all open.
take: Do it as a loop: on foot up and cable car down, or the reverse. Start at Liberty Square metro, walk down through the lanes to the baths, climb the marked steps past the statue to the ridge for the view — then, with an afternoon, drop into the Botanical Garden (ticketed, huge, quiet, with a waterfall) and come back up. Ride the cable car down to Rike Park at dusk and cross the Peace Bridge. The Old Town is safe and easy, but it is also where a newcomer meets the tourist economy: 'traditional' restaurants with laminated menus and touts, and unmarked taxis whose meter is a phone app set to fiction. Eat elsewhere, hail Bolt. Rustaveli Avenue above Freedom Square is closed to traffic for rehabilitation until about the end of November 2026 and has daily evening demonstrations by Parliament — walk around large crowds; that is a safety note, not a political one. Narikala's walls are shut: a long restoration that was still closed in August 2026, with no reopening date announced. The ridge, Kartlis Deda and the views are open — it is the fortress itself you cannot promise anyone.

sections.title: Don't miss
items: The cable car from Rike Park — pay with a Metromoney card, sold at any metro kiosk; the same card does metro and buses on one flat fare with 90 minutes of free transfers.
Kartlis Deda and the ridge viewpoints — the whole city, both banks, at once.
The National Botanical Garden below the fortress — a ticket, a waterfall, and the quietest hour in central Tbilisi.
The Jumah Mosque, Sioni cathedral and the Anchiskhati basilica — three faiths inside four hundred metres.
Tbilisoba, the city's birthday festival, fills the Old Town for a weekend in October — the date is announced only a few weeks ahead, so don't build a group around a guessed one.

title: Sololaki: courtyards, stairwells and the last of old Tiflis
tagline: Art-nouveau entrances with painted ceilings, 'Italian yards' hung with laundry and vines, and the neighbourhood every newcomer ends up living in or wishing they did.
when: a weekday morning when the doors are propped open; again after dark for the lit stairwells
why: Sololaki climbs the hill south-west of Freedom Square, and it was built in one burst between about 1880 and 1914 by Tbilisi's merchant families — Armenian, Georgian, Persian, German — who competed through their front doors. Behind those doors are stairwells with frescoed ceilings, wrought-iron banisters, stained glass and stucco that a century of communal living, earthquakes and neglect has faded rather than destroyed. The Kalantarov house on Machabeli Street, the Writers' House beside it, and the entrances up Asatiani, Lermontov and Amaghleba streets are the famous ones, but the point is to push a door that isn't locked and look up. The other Sololaki institution is the 'Italian yard' — the shared inner courtyard where a dozen households hang washing over a wooden gallery, grow a vine across the whole thing and argue between balconies. It is disappearing to renovation and short-term lets; go now.
take: Walk it slowly, from Freedom Square up Lado Asatiani to Machabeli and across to Betlemi, then up the Betlemi steps toward the ridge. Be a guest: these are people's homes, so no flash, no touching the plaster, a 'gamarjoba' to whoever is on the stairs, and back out if someone looks unhappy. Many entrances are now code-locked; the ones left open are the gift. Sololaki is also where a lot of our members will live — central, cheap-ish, and the cafés on Asatiani and around Gudiashvili Square are where you'll keep running into the same faces, which is how a community starts. Come back at night when the stairwell lamps are on. And a gentle word: don't call it 'the Old Town' to a local; Sololaki is its own thing and proud of it.

sections.title: Don't miss
items: The Kalantarov house (Machabeli 17) and the Writers' House garden (Machabeli 13) — the two grand ones.
Gudiashvili Square — restored, some say over-restored; the cafés around it are where Sololaki meets for coffee.
The Betlemi steps up toward Narikala's ridge — old churches, views and the last real courtyards.
Any door ajar on Asatiani, Lermontov or Amaghleba — look up first.
The 'Italian yards': ask a member with a local landlord for an introduction; a supra in one is the Tbilisi initiation.

title: Mtatsminda: the funicular, the Pantheon and the park on top
tagline: A 1905 funicular up the Holy Mountain, the graves of Georgia's writers halfway, a Soviet-era amusement park, and the whole city at your feet.
time: half a day, or an evening
when: an hour before sunset; the funicular runs late in summer
why: Mtatsminda — 'holy mountain' — is the ridge above Rustaveli Avenue with the television tower on it, and the funicular that climbs it has been running, with pauses, since 1905. It leaves from Chonkadze Street behind Rustaveli, stops halfway at the Pantheon — the terraced cemetery around St David's church where Georgia's poets, writers and public figures lie, Ilia Chavchavadze among them, along with Griboyedov and his Georgian wife — and ends at Mtatsminda Park: a Soviet amusement park rebuilt in the 2000s with a Ferris wheel on the cliff edge, a roller coaster, a big restaurant and lawns where families picnic. At 770 metres it is a few degrees cooler than the city, which in July matters. Look down and you read Tbilisi like a map: the river, the Old Town's roofs, the left bank, and on a clear day the Caucasus wall to the north with Kazbek in it. It is where the city goes on Sunday, and it costs almost nothing.
take: Ride up, walk down — or the reverse, because the walk is real: a path from the park drops through the pines to the Pantheon and on down the steps to Rustaveli in about forty minutes, and it is the best free hour in the city. The funicular sells rides on its own reloadable card, not Metromoney, from the lower station; park.ge gives one schedule all year — the funicular runs 11:00 to 22:30 daily, the food court to 23:00 — so a night ride means before half past ten. The park is free to enter and the rides are paid piecemeal, so a group can do as much or as little as it likes. The Pantheon is the stop most visitors skip and the one we'd insist on: give it twenty minutes and read the names. Rustaveli below is closed to cars for rehabilitation until late 2026, so come by metro (Rustaveli station) and walk up to Chonkadze.

sections.title: Don't miss
items: The Pantheon at the mid-station — Chavchavadze, Griboyedov and Nino Chavchavadze, and the church of St David.
The Ferris wheel on the cliff edge — the one ride worth paying for; ride it at dusk.
The lawns on the far side of the park for a picnic; bring your own.
The walking path down through the pines to the Pantheon and Rustaveli — our standard post-sunset descent.
The TV tower lit at night is the city's compass; if you can see it, you know where the centre is.

title: Vera, Vake and the café life
tagline: The two neighbourhoods where Tbilisi's laptop crowd, students and old intelligentsia drink coffee — a park with a war memorial at the top, and a city that changed fast after 2022.
when: weekday afternoons for the cafés; Saturday morning for Vake Park
why: Vera is the tangle of streets between Rustaveli and the Vere river gorge — old, hilly, full of nineteenth-century houses, with Kiacheli and Tarkhnishvili streets and the lanes around the Vera Garden turned into a strip of cafés, bakeries, wine bars and small restaurants. Vake, further west along Chavchavadze Avenue, was the Soviet professors' and officials' district and is now the most expensive part of the city: wide streets, plane trees, embassies, brunch places and boutiques, all leading up to Vake Park — Victory Park — with its war memorial, the long stairs, and the cable car up to Turtle Lake. Both changed fast after February 2022, when a large Russian-speaking arrival wave brought money, coworkings and a new café every week; rents rose, some Georgians resented it, and the communities mostly live side by side rather than together. It is a live subject; listen more than you talk.
take: This is where most of our first coffees happen, and where a newcomer sees the city's international side fastest. Pick a café in Vera with tables on the street, sit for two hours, and you'll hear Georgian, Russian, English and Turkish at the next four tables. For Vake, walk the length of Chavchavadze and climb the park's stairs to the memorial in the late afternoon, then come down through the lower tiers where the old men play nardi. Some cautions: Vake prices are Istanbul prices; neither district has a metro (walk from Rustaveli, take a bus, or Bolt), and Chavchavadze traffic is bad while Rustaveli is dug up. Learn 'gamarjoba' and 'madloba' and use them — being taken for a Russian speaker is the one thing that makes people cooler, and a word of Georgian dissolves it instantly. Keep the politics for people who raise it themselves.

sections.title: How to do it
items: Vera: the streets around Kiacheli, Tarkhnishvili and the Vera Garden — cafés, bakeries and small wine bars.
Vake: Chavchavadze Avenue from the university end to the park; the side streets (Abashidze, Paliashvili) have the quieter places.
Vake Park: climb the stairs to the war memorial; the lower park is families and nardi boards.
The Turtle Lake cable car leaves from the top edge of the park — see the Turtle Lake entry.
No metro here; Vera is a ten-minute walk from Rustaveli station, Vake is a bus or a Bolt.

title: Fabrika and the left bank: Marjanishvili after dark
tagline: A Soviet sewing factory turned hostel-and-courtyard, Aghmashenebeli's pedestrian stretch, and the side of the river where the younger city drinks.
when: Thursday to Saturday from 8pm; the courtyard is a daytime coworking too
why: Cross the river to the left bank and the city changes register: nineteenth-century Aghmashenebeli Avenue, built by German settlers and restored in stretches as 'New Tiflis' with a pedestrianised section of restaurants and terraces, Marjanishvili Square and its metro, and behind them the streets of Chugureti where the rents are lower and the bars are younger. Fabrika, at 8 Ninoshvili Street, is the anchor: a Soviet-era sewing factory that reopened in 2016 as a big hostel with a courtyard of bars, cafés, studios, a coworking space, a barber and shops, its walls covered in murals. It is not a secret — every backpacker in the Caucasus passes through — but it is genuinely where locals, nomads and travellers end up at the same long tables, and it runs markets, screenings and a Christmas fair in the yard through the year. Around it, the Marjanishvili lanes have the city's best cheap bars, with Fabrika's courtyard as the meeting point everyone can find.
take: Use Fabrika the way we do: as the place to say 'meet at eight in the courtyard' with people who don't know the city yet, because nobody gets lost and nobody has to book. Then leave. The good part is the second hour, when a local walks the group two streets over to a bar with eight seats and a man pouring chacha. Aghmashenebeli's pedestrian stretch is fine for a first walk and a terrace dinner with visiting parents; it is also where the restaurants aim at tourists, so eat one street back. Marjanishvili metro is at the door and the last trains run around midnight — after that it's Bolt. The area is safe and busy late; the usual rules apply about unmarked taxis and walking the embankment alone at 3am. In summer the courtyard is the coolest outdoor room in the city; in winter it moves inside and gets loud.

sections.title: How to do it
items: Fabrika, Ninoshvili 8 — the courtyard is free to enter; hostel, bars, coworking and shops around it.
Aghmashenebeli's pedestrian section — a terrace stretch for a first evening; eat a street back for value.
Marjanishvili metro is the nearest stop; last trains around midnight, leaving the termini about 23:50.
The Dry Bridge market is a fifteen-minute walk back toward the river — a Saturday pairing.
Weeknights are locals and long-term nomads; weekends bring the Old Town crowd across.

title: The Dry Bridge flea market
tagline: Soviet medals, Georgian enamel, cameras, carpets and a lot of things nobody needs, spread on the ground by the river every day and worth a Saturday every month.
when: a weekend late morning; it packs up in rain
why: The Dry Bridge crosses a channel of the Mtkvari that was filled in long ago, and since the early 1990s — when the Soviet collapse sent families out to sell what they had — the bridge and Dedaena Park below it have been Tbilisi's flea market. It never left. What's on the blankets now is a mix of the real and the reproduced: Soviet badges and medals, Red Army caps, Zenit cameras, samovars, Georgian minankari enamel jewellery, drinking horns, carpets, old photographs, coins, chess sets, Georgian and Russian books, sheet music, and at the park end a stretch of painters selling canvases. Prices start high for foreigners and come down with a smile and a walk-away; bargaining is expected and mostly good-natured. It runs every day of the year in some form, but the full market — with the old men and the good stuff — is a weekend late morning.
take: Go with no list and a little cash in small notes; the best thing about the Dry Bridge is not buying but talking, and the sellers, many of them pensioners, will tell you where a medal came from if you give them a minute. Treat militaria as history and buy accordingly — some are copies, and some countries frown on importing them. The enamel jewellery and the old photographs are what we'd actually take home. It is a natural first Smileys Saturday: meet at the bridge at eleven, wander, then walk across to the left bank for khinkali or up to Vera for coffee. It gets hot and shadeless by one in summer, and it thins out fast in rain. Nearest metro is Marjanishvili on the left bank, or a ten-minute walk down from Rustaveli.

sections.title: Don't miss
items: The badge-and-medal tables on the bridge itself — the history lesson is free even if you buy nothing.
Minankari (cloisonné enamel) jewellery — the best Georgian gift, and cheaper here than in the Old Town shops.
The painters at the park end; some are very good, most are fine, all will talk.
Old Tbilisi photographs and postcards — for anyone furnishing a flat.
Cash in small notes; walk away once and the price drops.

title: The Dezerter Bazaar: where the city actually shops
tagline: Tbilisi's central food market by the railway station — churchkhela, sulguni, spices, herbs by the armful, and a redevelopment plan that hangs over it.
when: a weekday morning before ten; it winds down by mid-afternoon
why: The name comes from the 1920s, when deserters from the army sold their kit here; what it is now is the city's belly, a sprawl of halls and street stalls around Tsinamdzgvrishvili Street a block from Station Square (Vagzlis Moedani). Inside and around it: cheese women with towers of sulguni and imeruli, honey in jars, tarragon and coriander by the armful, tkemali plum sauce, ajika, Svan salt, walnuts, dried fruit, churchkhela strings of walnut in grape must, tomatoes and cucumbers that still taste of something, butchers, fish from the Black Sea, and the Georgian spice blends — khmeli suneli, utskho suneli — sold from open sacks. It is loud, real and cheap, and everyone in it will feed you a sample. The honest caveat: in 2024 the city presented plans to demolish part of the market for a shopping centre, deadlines have come and gone, and as of this writing the traders don't know either.
take: Come hungry and early, with a bag and small notes. Start in the cheese hall, taste before you buy, and let the vendors lead — 'this one, from Imereti, try'. Load up on churchkhela, spices and a jar of ajika for the flat; those are the things that make a newcomer's kitchen Georgian in a week. Then walk out with a khachapuri from one of the bakeries on the edge and eat it standing up. It's a good group outing precisely because it isn't designed for us, and a Georgian member makes it three times better. Practicalities: Station Square metro, one block west; open daily from early morning and quiet by mid-afternoon; watch bags in the crush as anywhere. Ask on the group before planning a visit. The city has been promising to demolish the main hall and put a shopping centre on it since 2024, and the date has slipped every year since — but it could start any season, and when the hall goes the stalls will shift to the surrounding streets.

sections.title: Don't miss
items: The cheese hall — sulguni, imeruli, guda, and smoked sulguni for the road.
Churchkhela and tklapi (fruit leather) — buy from the woman who made them, not the ones in plastic.
The spice sacks: khmeli suneli, utskho suneli (blue fenugreek), Svan salt.
Tkemali and ajika in unlabelled jars — ask which is the hot one.
Metro: Station Square (Vagzlis Moedani), then one block west.

title: Khinkali, khachapuri and the supra
tagline: How Georgia eats: soup dumplings you hold by the knot, cheese bread with an egg in it, and the long, toasted, tamada-led dinner that turns strangers into a table.
when: any evening; a supra needs a Georgian host and a Saturday
why: Georgian food is the strongest argument for living here, and it's cheap enough that a Smileys dinner for ten costs what four people pay in Istanbul. Khinkali are the pleated dumplings from the mountains: minced meat and broth in a twist of dough, eaten by hand — hold the knot, bite a corner, drink the soup, eat the rest, leave the knot on the plate as a count. Khachapuri is the cheese bread, and every region has one: the boat-shaped adjaruli with a raw egg and butter stirred in at the table, the round imeruli, the double-layered megruli. Around them: pkhali (walnut-and-vegetable pâtés), badrijani (aubergine rolled around walnut), lobio beans in a clay pot, mtsvadi grilled on vine wood, chakapuli of lamb and tarragon in spring, and always bread, tkemali and a jug of house wine. The supra is the feast form — a table run by a tamada who leads the toasts in order, and no one drinks outside a toast.
take: Learn the khinkali grip on your first night at a plain khinkali house, not a tourist restaurant: the place with a paper menu, a TV and a queue of taxi drivers is the right one. Order five per person to start, kalakuri (city-style, with herbs) and mtiuluri (mountain, plain), with a beer or a jug of white. Then work through the rest over a month. We name no restaurants: the city turns over fast, the Old Town has too many 'traditional' places with laminated menus, and every Georgian member has a different aunt's version. Ask on the group. When you're invited to a supra, go, and the rules matter: don't drink until the tamada toasts, don't toast with beer, say a few words when it comes round to you, and eat slowly — it is a five-hour form. Say 'gaumarjos'. That dinner is the whole reason we exist.

sections.title: The Georgian table
items: Khinkali — by hand, by the knot; kalakuri with herbs or mtiuluri plain. Count the knots.
Khachapuri adjaruli — stir the egg and butter into the cheese before it sets; share one.
Pkhali and badrijani — the walnut starters that carry the table.
Mtsvadi and lobio — the grill and the beans; chakapuli in spring.
The supra: wait for the tamada, wine not beer for toasts, and 'gaumarjos' is the word.

title: Qvevri wine: the amber-wine bars of Sololaki and Vera
tagline: Wine fermented in buried clay for eight thousand years, now poured by the glass in cellars and shops around Freedom Square — the best cheap education in the city.
when: early evening, before dinner; the good bars fill after nine
why: Georgia has the oldest evidence of winemaking anywhere — residue in clay from around 6000 BC — and the method never stopped: grapes, skins and stems go into a qvevri, a big clay vessel buried to the neck, and ferment underground for months. White grapes made this way come out amber, tannic and unlike anything from a steel tank; UNESCO listed the method in 2013. The country has more than five hundred native grapes — rkatsiteli, mtsvane, kisi and saperavi are the ones you'll meet first — and a family-winery revival since the 2000s means the natural-wine movement here is not a fashion but the default. In Tbilisi that translates into wine bars and bottle shops pouring by the glass with a plate of cheese and bread: DADI just off Freedom Square, 8000 Vintages on Tabukashvili Street and in Vake, and a rotating cast of cellars along Galaktion Tabidze, Asatiani and around Gudiashvili Square in Sololaki, and the Vera lanes.
take: Start with a flight, not a bottle: ask for three ambers — a rkatsiteli, a kisi, a mtsvane — and one saperavi, and let the person pouring talk; in the good bars they know the winemaker. This is the perfect Smileys midweek: six people, a cellar table, two hours, and the conversation goes somewhere because the wine is strange enough to discuss. Then buy a bottle from a small family producer for your next supra — bringing wine is always right. Two honest notes: house wine by the jug in a restaurant is usually fine and very cheap, while a named qvevri bottle in a bar is Istanbul money; and chacha, the grape spirit, is offered everywhere and is a different evening. Vino Underground on Galaktion Tabidze was the pioneer natural-wine bar from 2012 — Check it is still open before sending a group; listings are inconsistent. The bars above were open as of mid-2026, but the scene turns over fast enough that a year-old recommendation is a coin toss — ask on the group first.

sections.title: How to do it
items: DADI, off Freedom Square — a shop and bar with a big by-the-glass list; a good first stop.
8000 Vintages, Tabukashvili Street (also Vake) — bottle shop with tastings; buy the supra bottle here.
The cellars of Galaktion Tabidze and Asatiani streets, Sololaki — walk, read the boards, pick one with a table free.
Order ambers first: rkatsiteli, kisi, mtsvane; then a saperavi to finish.
Kakheti is two hours away for the source — see the Sighnaghi entry.

title: A night at Bassiani
tagline: Techno in a drained Soviet swimming pool under the football stadium — one of the world's serious clubs, with a door that asks why you came.
when: Friday or Saturday; buy tickets online days ahead for big lineups
why: Bassiani opened in 2014 in the empty swimming pool beneath Dinamo Arena on Tsereteli Avenue, and within a few years it was on every list of the world's best clubs — not for the sound system alone but for what it meant here: a space where queer Georgians, ravers and the city's counterculture could exist in a conservative country. That earned it a police raid in May 2018 and a dance protest outside Parliament that reopened it. It is still open, still selective, and still the reason a certain kind of person moves to Tbilisi. The programme is techno, mostly resident-led, with international guests; Horoom Nights are the queer-focused programming and the door is strictest then. Around it a scene grew: KHIDI under a bridge on the left bank, Mtkvarze in an old riverside restaurant, and Left Bank. Expect a queue, an ID check, stickers over your phone cameras, and no filming inside.
take: Do it once even if clubs aren't your thing, because it explains the city. Buy the ticket on bassiani.com in advance, go after one in the morning (the room doesn't fill before), go in a small group rather than a stag party, dress like you're going dancing and not to a rooftop, and answer the door honestly — they may ask who's playing and why you came, and they turn away people who seem to be there to gawk. It is not a Smileys 'event' in the usual sense — we don't book tables, there aren't any — but four or five who go together and leave together is right. Bolt home; the streets around Station Square at 6am are fine but empty. The club's politics are its own and the climate around Parliament is tense this year; keep your phone in your pocket and your opinions among friends. Read the night's own event page for the door policy and any age or ID rule — it changes by night, and the door is the whole reputation.

sections.title: How to do it
items: Tickets on bassiani.com for a specific night; big lineups sell out days ahead — no walk-ups then.
Arrive after 1am; the door may ask why you came — answer straight, and don't come in a big loud group.
ID, camera stickers, no filming. Horoom Nights are the queer-focused programme; the door is strictest then.
KHIDI, Mtkvarze and Left Bank are the other rooms — Check each is open this season; venues here open and close fast, and the protest years shut several of them for months at a time.
Station Square metro by day; Bolt at night.

title: Mtskheta: Jvari, Svetitskhoveli and the meeting of the rivers
tagline: The old capital twenty minutes north — a sixth-century church on a cliff above two rivers and the cathedral where the country was baptised, both UNESCO, both a marshrutka from Didube.
when: a weekday morning; Jvari in late-afternoon light if you can stretch it
why: Mtskheta was Georgia's capital for the best part of a thousand years before Tbilisi, and it is where, in the 330s, King Mirian's conversion made Georgia one of the first Christian states. Two buildings carry that: Svetitskhoveli cathedral (eleventh century, on a fourth-century site), the seat of the Georgian church, which holds Christ's robe under its central pillar by tradition and is still where patriarchs are crowned and buried; and Jvari, the small sixth-century cross church on the bluff opposite, above the point where the Aragvi meets the Mtkvari — the view Lermontov wrote into 'Mtsyri' and the image on every Georgian's phone. With Samtavro convent they form the Historical Monuments of Mtskheta World Heritage site. The town itself has been restored into a pedestrian core of souvenir stalls and restaurants; it's pretty and a little staged. The churches are the point.
take: Take the metro to Didube and find the Mtskheta marshrutka in the yard (they leave when full; a fixed-schedule shuttle started in January 2026 — every forty minutes, 09:00 to 18:00, 3 GEL). Svetitskhoveli first, early, before the tour buses; cover shoulders and knees, scarves at the door, no shorts. Then a taxi up to Jvari — it's on the far side of the river and there's no bus — and walk the ridge below the church for the confluence view. Back down for lunch on the river; Mtskheta's restaurants are honest if unremarkable. It is our easiest half-day out of the city, the one we do with every visiting parent, and it pairs with the Dezerter Bazaar or an afternoon in town. Group logistics are simple: eight people fit in one shared van. Dress and behave as if the churches are in use, because they are.

sections.title: How to do it
items: Didube metro, then the Mtskheta marshrutka from the yard; about half an hour.
Svetitskhoveli at opening, then Samtavro if you have time; scarves and long trousers.
A taxi up to Jvari and back — agree the wait time before you get in.
The confluence view from the ridge below Jvari, late afternoon for the light.
Back in the city by mid-afternoon: this is a half-day, not a day.

title: Sighnaghi and a day in Kakheti
tagline: The wine region two hours east: a walled hill town over the Alazani plain, family cellars, Bodbe convent, and the harvest in September and October.
time: a full day, or a night
when: September–October for rtveli, the harvest; a weekday if you can
why: Kakheti is where most Georgian wine is made, and Sighnaghi is its postcard: an eighteenth-century walled town on a ridge with pastel houses and wooden balconies restored in the 2000s, looking out over the Alazani valley to the wall of the Caucasus. Below it are villages of family cellars — marani — where the qvevri are buried under the floor and the tasting is at the kitchen table. Two kilometres away is Bodbe, the convent where St Nino, who converted Georgia, is buried, with gardens, a spring and pilgrims. In September and October comes rtveli, the harvest: grapes pressed by foot, must poured into the qvevri, and every village hosting a supra in the yard. Sighnaghi is also Georgia's 'city of love' — there's a round-the-clock registry office — and it has become touristy in the same way as the Old Town, but the valley behind it hasn't.
take: Marshrutkas leave from the yard beside Samgori metro on a fixed schedule through the day; be there thirty minutes early for a seat, and the ride is a little over two hours. That works for a day, but the version we love is a shared car with five or six people that stops at a family winery on the way (a Georgian member arranges this by phone; there is no app), walks Sighnaghi's walls before lunch, does Bodbe, and drives back at dusk — or stays the night in a guesthouse and returns by the first van. During rtveli, ask a Kakhetian member whether a family needs hands: a day picking, a night at the table. Drink less than you're poured; the driver drinks nothing, and Georgian roads at night reward that. Be a guest, not a customer — bring something, take your shoes off at the door, and say thank you in the toast.

sections.title: Don't miss
items: The town walls and the viewpoint over the Alazani plain toward the Caucasus.
Bodbe convent, a half-hour walk from town — St Nino's tomb and the spring.
A family marani in a village below the town — arranged by a member, not a tour desk.
Rtveli in September–October: ask on the group whether a family wants pickers.
Samgori metro for the marshrutka; the last one back is early evening, and nobody publishes the time — ask the driver on the way out.

title: Up the Georgian Military Highway: Gudauri, Kazbegi and Gergeti Trinity
tagline: The road north over the Jvari Pass to Stepantsminda, a church on a shoulder under a 5,000-metre volcano — and the ski resort on the way that runs from late December.
time: a full day, better a night
when: September–October for the walk; late December to April for skiing; check the pass in winter
why: The Georgian Military Highway is the imperial road north from Tbilisi to Vladikavkaz, and its first 150 kilometres are the best day out in the country: the Aragvi reservoir and Ananuri fortress, the climb to Gudauri at 2,200 metres, the Soviet-era friendship monument on the cliff, the Jvari Pass at 2,400, and down to Stepantsminda (Kazbegi), a mountain town under Mount Kazbek, 5,047 metres and often snow-plumed. Above it on a grassy shoulder at 2,170 metres stands Gergeti Trinity, a fourteenth-century church that is the most photographed thing in Georgia and deserves it. A paved road has run to it since 2018, so it is a taxi ride or a two-hour hike from town. Gudauri, on the way, is Georgia's main ski resort — wide, treeless, above the clouds, with lifts that in recent seasons opened between 21 and 27 December and ran to April, and paragliding and hiking from the same slopes in summer.
take: In September, go for the walk: the hike from Stepantsminda to Gergeti takes two hours up through the birch woods, and the valley walk beyond toward the Gergeti glacier is as far as most of us go. Stay the night — the light on Kazbek at dawn is the point — in one of the town's guesthouses. Transport is a marshrutka from Didube (three hours, a queue, an Ananuri stop) or a shared car for five, which is what we do. In winter, Gudauri is the reason: under two hours' drive, cheap by Alpine standards, with beginners' slopes and serious off-piste. Two things to check before promising anyone anything. The 2026–27 Gudauri opening date: the resort operator (mta.ski) normally announces it in December and not before, so in autumn nobody knows it, us included. And the road: the Jvari Pass closes for avalanche risk several times each winter and Kazbegi is cut off for days most years, while the new Kvesheti–Kobi tunnel road — still not open as of September 2026, due in stages through 2026–27 — may change all of that. Never book a non-refundable night north of the pass in January.

sections.title: How to do it
items: Didube for the Kazbegi marshrutka, or a shared car from the group — three hours with an Ananuri stop.
Gergeti Trinity: two hours on foot from Stepantsminda, or a 4x4 taxi from the square; dress for a church.
Stay the night; watch Kazbek at dawn, and walk toward the Gergeti glacier if the legs allow.
Gudauri in winter: lifts ran 10:00–17:00 in past seasons; the opening date goes up on mta.ski in December; the Kobi cable car has been the bypass when the pass shuts.
September to October is the honest window; the pass and the weather make the rules from November to April.

title: Turtle Lake, the Kojori ridge and the walk back into town
tagline: A lake above Vake by cable car, a pine ridge with an eleventh-century fortress twenty kilometres out, and the hill walks that stitch them to the city.
when: a weekend morning before ten; September and October are the best months
why: Turtle Lake (Kus Tba) is a small reservoir in the hills above Vake Park, reached by a cable car from the top of the park, rebuilt in 2016 and costing about a metro ride, or by a stiff path through the woods. Around it: a running loop, a swimming platform in summer, cafés, pedalos, and the Open-Air Museum of Ethnography below the road — real houses moved here from every region of Georgia. It is the city's Sunday. Behind and above, the ridge continues south-west toward Kojori, a hill village at 1,300 metres that was the summer retreat of Tbilisi's families under the tsars, with the ruined Kojori fortress on a crag above it and the tiny Udzo monastery on the hillside beyond, looking back over the whole Tbilisi bowl and north to the Caucasus. The classic walk goes from Kojori over the ridge past Udzo and down to Turtle Lake or Mtatsminda — four to five hours, marked in parts, downhill in the right direction.
take: The easy version is Turtle Lake on a Saturday morning: up from Vake, a loop, coffee, the Ethnography museum on the way down, back for lunch — a Smileys regular. The cable car from Chavchavadze is the way up when it runs, but it has been out for maintenance since December 2025 with nothing published since, so check it the evening before or plan on a Bolt to the top. The proper version is the ridge: a Bolt or the Kojori bus out to the village early, the fortress first for the view, then the path over to Udzo and down to the lake; bring water, real shoes and a downloaded map, because the signage comes and goes and so does the phone signal. Don't do it at August midday — Tbilisi's heat is dry and brutal and the ridge has little shade — and not after rain, when the clay track turns to grease. Kojori itself is a ten-minute stroll of dachas and a monastery, not a destination; the walk is. Bus 380 from Baratashvili Street by Freedom Square is the direct one — 316 toward Kiketi stops there too — roughly every forty minutes from 07:00 to 23:00, 1 GEL, about three quarters of an hour. The Ethnography museum runs Tuesday to Sunday, 10:00 to 18:00, and is closed on Mondays.

sections.title: How to do it
items: Turtle Lake cable car from the top of Vake Park — Metromoney, early morning to late evening; the walk up is a good forty minutes.
The Open-Air Museum of Ethnography on the road below the lake — a ticket, and the best hour of Georgian architecture in the city.
Kojori fortress, then the path to Udzo monastery and the viewpoint — the ridge walk's spine.
Water, shoes, an offline map; no shade, and the track is slick after rain.
Finish at Turtle Lake, or drop to Mtatsminda Park and take the funicular down.
